blocks.text: 我们很高兴地宣布，vLLM 已实现 Mistral Large 4 的 day-0 支持。Mistral Large 4 是 Mistral 推出的新一代前沿混合专家（MoE）原生多模态模型。它把 DeepSeek 风格的稀疏注意力栈（MLA 加 DSA top-k 索引器）与多项新架构特性结合在一起：跨层 KV 共享、NoPE 层、SSMax 和 LeRoPE。模型自带 DSpark 投机解码草稿器和 Pixtral 视觉编码器。

inlines.text: 72 层 MoE，128 个路由专家（top-4）加 1 个共享专家，隐藏维度 6144。注意力采用 MLA（KV LoRA 秩 512，RoPE 维度 64），并配有 DSA 稀疏索引器，每个查询选取 top 2048 个 key。总参数 1 万亿，每 token 激活 490 亿（含嵌入层和输出层为 520 亿）。
FP8（块缩放权重）和 NVFP4（专家用 NVFP4，注意力/共享专家用 FP8）。两者默认都使用 FP8 潜在 KV 缓存（
Pixtral 视觉编码器处理图像输入，支持每个提示词包含多张图片。
内置 DSpark 草稿器（3 层滑动窗口 MLA，深度 3），每步接受约 2.9 个 token，在 TP8 上输出吞吐约提升 2 倍。
DCP 在 TP8 上带来约 7.9 倍的 KV 容量。PCP+DCP 预填充把首 token 时间（TTFT）最多缩短 1.6 倍。DSpark 在两种模式下都能工作。
NIXL 预填充/解码（P/D）分离，支持 DP/EP、TP 和 PCP×DCP 预填充节点，两侧都启用 DSpark。
主机内存稀疏 KV 卸载，现已支持跨层 KV 共享。
在 AMD Instinct MI350 系列 GPU 上通过 ROCm 实现 day-0 支持，包括 DSpark、图像输入和 MXFP4 专家的专家并行。

NVFP4 不以质量换速度。在多模态、长上下文、智能体编程、业务自动化和网络安全评测中，它在每项任务上与 FP8 的差距都在 2.1 分以内，平均差异为 −0.3 分。token 消耗也相当：平均补全 token 数与 FP8 相差约 4% 以内。它还更快、更省：在 TP8 下，不使用投机解码时 NVFP4 每 token 解码速度比 FP8 快 1.08–1.19 倍（启用 DSpark 时为 1.18–1.22 倍），KV 缓存容量约为 1.5 倍。

blocks.text: 何时使用 DCP。DCP 用每步延迟换 KV 容量。在同样的 8x GB300 NVFP4 部署和工作负载下（无投机解码），DCP8 每 token 的解码速度比 TP8 慢约 16–28%：8k 输入时 c1 TPOT 为 11.1 vs 8.7 ms，60k 时为 11.4 vs 9.1 ms。在最多 128 个 8k–60k token 的并发请求下，TP8 的 3.6M token 池从来不是瓶颈，因此 TP8 在那里吞吐更高。一旦 KV 成为限制，DCP8 才划算：超长上下文，或大量并发的长生命周期会话。在我们的 agentic P/D 运行中（约 100k token 会话），一个 TP4 DCP4 解码节点在 32 个会话下把 TTFT 保持在 0.7 s，而普通 TP4 解码节点 KV 耗尽，TTFT 攀升到 15 s。

blocks.text: DSpark 投机解码

ML4 在 checkpoint 中内置了一个 DSpark drafter（mtp_dspark.* 个张量，以及 params.json 中的一个 mtp 块）。DSpark 是一种并行 drafter：一个小型非因果 transformer 在一次前向中提出一个块内所有 draft 位置。它以从目标模型第 1、18、36、54、71 层引出的隐藏状态为条件。ML4 的 drafter 还增加了：

一个门控循环状态（rank 512）在各 draft 位置间运行，因此每个位置的 logits 都依赖于它之前 draft 出的 token；

blocks.text: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder.

NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. blocks.text: When to use DCP. DCP trades per-step latency for KV capacity. On the same 8x GB300 NVFP4 deployment and workload (no spec decoding), DCP8 decodes about 16–28% slower per token than TP8: c1 TPOT is 11.1 vs 8.7 ms at 8k input and 11.4 vs 9.1 ms at 60k. With up to 128 concurrent requests of 8k–60k tokens, TP8's 3.6M-token pool is never the bottleneck, so TP8 delivers more throughput there. DCP8 pays off once KV is the limit: very long contexts, or many concurrent long-lived sessions. In our agentic P/D runs (~100k-token sessions), a TP4 DCP4 decode node kept TTFT at 0.7 s at 32 sessions, where a plain TP4 decode node ran out of KV and climbed to 15 s.

Under PCP the MLA KV-cache write first all-gathers its inputs across PCP ranks, and that gather depends on the batch's prefill/decode split. ML4 ships a DSpark drafter inside the checkpoint (mtp_dspark.* tensors and an mtp block in params.json). DSpark is a parallel drafter: a small non-causal transformer proposes all draft positions of a block in one forward pass. It conditions on hidden states tapped from target layers 1, 18, 36, 54 and 71. ML4's drafter adds:

inlines.text: ML4 ships a DSpark drafter inside the checkpoint (

). DSpark is a parallel drafter: a small non-causal transformer proposes all draft positions of a block in one forward pass. It conditions on hidden states tapped from target layers 1, 18, 36, 54 and 71. ML4's drafter adds:
a gated recurrent state (rank 512) runs across the draft positions, so each position's logits depend on the tokens drafted before it;
each draft slot gets its own learned input embedding instead of one shared mask token;
3 MLA layers with a 2048-token window and a BF16 KV cache, in their own KV cache group. The Triton MLA backend gained sliding-window decode for them.

blocks.text: DSpark + DCP. Before this work, sliding-window MLA drafts could not run under DCP. Now the draft's small window cache (3 layers × ~2k tokens, about 7 MB per request) is replicated on every DCP rank, while the target cache stays DCP-sharded. The cost is KV capacity: under DCP8 each 64-token draft block holds a block ID whose target pages cover 512 tokens. At 64k context, capacity falls to about 0.69x of plain DCP8. That limit doesn't bind at max_num_seqs 128 below ~99k average context.

blocks.text: AITER. VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 runs vLLM's hot paths on AITER, AMD's kernel library: the fused MoE (the MXFP4 experts on two-stage FlyDSL kernels), the block-FP8 and bf16 GEMMs, the MLA decode kernels, RMSNorm and the tensor-parallel custom all-reduce. The ROCm image ships AITER tuning tables for this model's MoE and GEMM shapes, which AITER merges with its own at startup; at TP4 they raise output throughput 9–16% at 1–8 concurrent requests. Two more settings help on top: VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_TRITON_SPARSE_MLA=1 runs the sparse MLA on AITER's Triton kernel, and AITER_CUSTOM_AR_MAX_SIZE=134217728 keeps the all-reduces of large prefill steps (up to 128 MiB) on AITER's custom all-reduce. Together they raise output throughput a further 2–5% at TP4 and lower time to first token 5–7%. Both commands below set all three.

blocks.text: Specialized decode. For latency-bound serving, --additional-config '{"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}' runs every MoE layer of a 1-, 2- or 4-request decode step as one persistent FlyDSL kernel launch. The launch fuses attention, the indexer, the router, the MXFP4 experts and both tensor-parallel all-reduces. On MI350X at TP4 it lowers per-token decode latency 1.5× at one request and 1.1× at four compared with vLLM's standard decode on the same GPUs. It composes with DSpark: a single request's verify block runs on the fused kernels, for 2.9× lower per-token latency than the standard decode without speculation. Larger batches and prefill run the standard path. It runs on the default FP8 KV cache, requires TP4 and VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT_ACT=a4w4, and refuses to start otherwise, giving the reason. The kernel is adapted from ROCm ATOM's GLM-5.2 fused decode.

ROCm implementation details

Sparse MLA on AITER. On ROCm, ML4's sparse MLA runs on the ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE backend. The indexer's top-2048 positions are converted to global cache slots, and each query token becomes its own entry in the slot stream. AITER's MLA decode kernel then reads that stream in persistent mode, with work-split metadata built ahead of time to balance the load across CUs. AITER's MLA kernels take a multiple of 16 heads: TP4 gives exactly 16 of ML4's 64 heads per GPU, while TP8's 8 are padded to 16. VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_TRITON_SPARSE_MLA=1 switches to AITER's Triton sparse-MLA kernel instead, which needs no head padding and no separate FP8 copy of the query. NoPE layers on the bf16 cache have no RoPE part for AITER's kernel to read, so they run on vLLM's ragged Triton sparse-attention kernels.

blocks.text: DSA indexer on AITER. A fused Triton kernel quantizes each indexer key to FP8 with one scale and writes it into the indexer cache, 132 bytes per token per indexer layer. Within a cache block, keys are stored in 16×16 tiles, the layout AITER's paged reader expects. A single layout rule is shared by the writer and every reader (insert, prefill gather and paged logits), so they cannot disagree. Prefill scores run on AITER's fp8_mqa_logits and decode scores on AITER's paged MQA-logits kernel, both reading FP8 keys. The top-2048 comes from AITER's indexer top-k where it supports the shape, and from vLLM's top_k_per_row otherwise. Shared-indexer layers reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, as on other platforms.

blocks.text: FP8 latent cache. ROCm has no fp8_ds_mla layout, so when the checkpoint asks for an FP8 KV cache, ROCm uses a plain E4M3 cache instead. All 576 latent dimensions (512 NoPE and 64 RoPE) are stored as FP8 with one per-tensor scale, 576 bytes per token per layer, against 656 for fp8_ds_mla and 1,152 for bf16. The query is quantized to FP8 too, so AITER's kernel runs FP8 × FP8. With 63 cache-owning layers plus the indexer, a token takes 42,096 bytes, against 78,384 in bf16: the 1.86× KV capacity in the AMD section.

blocks.text: MXFP4 experts at load, one layer at a time. With VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT=mxfp4, the checkpoint loader is unchanged: it still loads block-FP8 expert weights with their block scales. Their parameters start on the meta device, and the layerwise loader materializes one layer at a time. As soon as a layer's experts are loaded, each expert is dequantized to bf16 and re-quantized to MXFP4 (E2M1 values, one E8M0 scale per 32 values), and that layer's FP8 copy is freed. Peak memory is the MXFP4 model plus one layer of FP8 experts, which is what lets the 1T model load on four GPUs. The weight error is about the same as quantizing the bf16 weights to MXFP4 directly. The experts then run on AITER's fused MoE: two-stage FlyDSL kernels with FP8 activations for a8w4, or MXFP4 × MXFP4 for a4w4.

blocks.text: Fail-stop. A persistent kernel that waits on peer GPUs must never hang the server. Every in-kernel wait gives up after 10 seconds, and giving up sets a sticky fault word on every rank, which ends the other ranks' waits at once. After every forward, a device-side assert checks the word before logits are computed. If the word is set, the step's remaining work never runs, the worker aborts and the engine stops, so no token from a failed step reaches a client. The check costs about 1 µs per launch.

blocks.text: TPU

Mistral Large 4 runs on TPU v7x from day 0 with vllm-torchtpu, including support for the Pixtral vision encoder. Our validated configuration combines intra-host tensor parallelism with cross-host data parallelism with expert parallelism across 16 TPU v7x chips.

The TPU implementation relies on vllm-torchtpu's sparse MLA and DSA indexer Pallas kernels, extending MLA with cross-layer KV cache sharing. We store the MLA latent KV cache in FP8 and support FP8 weight and activation quantization for dense linear projections. Routed experts use weight-only FP4 quantization (W4A16).
